extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; paleontologists; evolutionary biologists; graduate students
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative criteria and standards the chapter uses to judge whether a research program (e.g., punctuated equilibrium) or an approach (model-based paleontology) can found an autonomous theoretical discipline. Emphasizes problem-selection, evidential standards, modeling vs. inductivism, and the need for alternative explanatory forms to population genetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify a set of related scientific problems with high demand
rubrics_metrics.description: A candidate disciplinary program must 'identify a set of related scientific problems whose solution achieved sufficiently high demand' (i.e., problems others care to have solved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that failure to satisfy this criterion (not producing problems in sufficiently high demand) explains why punctuated equilibrium did not found a new discipline. Examples: if the phenomena the program highlights are already well understood theoretically, demand is low. Scoring note: ask whether the program raises novel, unresolved questions that practitioners across relevant fields want answered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive or clear observational access to phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The discipline should have some empirical phenomena to which its practitioners have special or exclusive observational access (e.g., paleontologists' access to fossil patterns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book frames 'exclusive observational access' as one of two possible bases for disciplinary autonomy; if the community lacks exclusive access, disciplinary claims are weakened. Example: paleontologists arguably had an advantage authenticating punctuated equilibrium because it is a fossil pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop an independent form of solution (alternative explanatory framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim autonomy, a field must 'develop a new form of solution to evolutionary problems' that is genuinely alternative to the dominant explanatory framework (here, population genetics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance stresses the need for an alternative explanatory approach with adequate precision and generality — e.g., 'species as particles' or other model forms. Anti-pattern: proposing a re-labeling or restatement that is reducible to the prevailing theory without adding independent mechanisms or predictive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-centered approach: construct testable models fitted to fossil patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmaking strategy should be model-centered: 'construct models of evolutionary processes and then fit them to fossil patterns,' because 'laws must be based on immanent processes that produce events, not on the events themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts model-based methods with pure inductivism. Guidance: produce simple, mechanism-disclosing models whose predictions can be compared to geographic, stratigraphic, and morphologic fossil data. Example quote: 'the paleontologist can approach the fossil record and ask... Are observed patterns ... consistent with the consequences of a particular theory of speciation?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject naive inductivism; acknowledge theory-ladenness of observation
rubrics_metrics.description: One must reject the 'inductivist' view that objective fact alone generates laws; instead acknowledge that observation is theory-laden and intentionally proliferate competing models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter warns against the 'vicious circle' where unacknowledged theoretical commitments make every new datum seem to confirm the prevailing theory. Recommended practice: explicitly state interpretive theories, develop multiple models to expose theory-dependence, and test model predictions against data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show phenomena are not artifacts of preservation/taphonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about fossil patterns (e.g., stasis) must demonstrate that the pattern is not merely an artifact of imperfect preservation or sampling biases in the fossil record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text discusses the counterargument that morphological stability may reflect non-preservation of change rather than true stasis (Futuyma 1987). Guidance: account for taphonomic processes and alternative explanations before treating patterns as biological facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate that phenomena require biological (not purely statistical) explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that the fossil pattern records a fact about evolutionary process that requires biological explanation rather than being fully explained by statistical or sampling arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author credits Eldredge and Gould with elevating fossil patterns (like stasis) to problems demanding biological explanation. Scoring: evaluate whether an explanation invokes causal biological mechanisms (e.g., stabilizing selection, speciation dynamics) rather than only statistical or taphonomic accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure novelty: phenomena and explanations are not already entailed by existing theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed program must pick out phenomena or explanations that are not already contained within existing theoretical frameworks (e.g., Simpson's quantum evolution, Fisherian stabilizing selection, or standard population genetics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter argues punctuated equilibrium often failed this test because its phenomena and mechanisms were arguably present in prior work. Anti-pattern: presenting a phenomenon as revolutionary when it is a deductive consequence of accepted theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link proposed mechanisms to general explanatory scope (theoretical relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the proposed mechanism(s) can plausibly account for broader classes of evolutionary change and thus have theoretical consequences beyond isolated cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gould and Eldredge's claim that understanding punctuated equilibrium would 'exhaust' what there is to know about evolutionary change is discussed as an aspirational move. Guidance: demonstrate generality — how the mechanism scales or applies across taxa, time scales, or phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce testable predictions about geographic, stratigraphic, and morphological distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorizing should generate concrete predictions about observable patterns (e.g., geographic/stratigraphic distributions, rates and directions of morphological change) that can be assessed in the fossil record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Eldredge and Gould's quote: paleontologists should ask whether observed patterns are 'consistent with the consequences of a particular theory of speciation.' Models should yield observable signatures for empirical testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate explanatory sufficiency vis-à-vis population genetics
rubrics_metrics.description: The new approach must show it can satisfy explanatory demands that population genetics either cannot or does not satisfactorily address, or else justify why an alternative explanatory level is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates reasons population genetics held default status (empirical success, lack of alternatives, reductionist bias). A successful paleontological approach must confront and overcome these bases — e.g., show unique predictive success, conceptual independence, or empirical domains where population genetics is insufficient.
